notes:
Below are verse-by-verse notes on Hebrews 11 from the sources I could reach.

**What I couldn't cover.** My search allowance ran out before I reached any Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org) or Orthodox (oca.org) pages, NET Bible notes, or bibleodyssey.org, so none of those appear. The Enduring Word page (David Guzik) cut off part-way through v. 16. For vv. 17–29 I used the summary that appeared in search results and Guzik's older study guide on Blue Letter Bible. For several later verses, Wesley is the only source I have.

**Where traditions differ.** In what I read, the only clear disagreements are v. 1 (Wesley vs. Word-Faith), v. 21 (Protestant writers arguing against an old Catholic reading) and v. 35 (Catholics vs. Protestants on 2 Maccabees). I did not find Protestant traditions disagreeing with each other on any verse.

---

**v. 1**
- **Wesley (Methodist):** This definition includes justifying faith, but not *as* justifying, because faith justifies only through its link to Christ, and Christ isn't named here. Faith gives a kind of present reality to what God has promised. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm
- **Adam Clarke (Methodist):** These are the effects of justifying faith: God's peace rests on it, and the Spirit pours God's love into the heart.  https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/hebrews/11-1.html
- **Guzik (Enduring Word):** Faith is the "sense" that gives evidence of the unseen world, as eyesight does for the material world. It is not a blind leap or bare intellectual belief. It goes beyond reason but does not contradict it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-11/
- **Ellicott:** Most Church Fathers read the word "substance" literally: faith makes hoped-for things real to us. Chrysostom put it this way: "The resurrection has not yet taken place, but faith substantiates (ὑφίστησιν) it in our souls." https://biblehub.com/hebrews/11-1.htm
- **GotQuestions:** The verse is not a complete definition of faith. It picks out two aspects to introduce the list of examples. The Greek word is variously translated "assurance," "confidence" or "reality."  https://www.gotquestions.org/faith-substance-things-hoped-for.html
- **Word of Faith (as Precept Austin, quoting Norman Geisler, presents it):** Word-Faith teachers take "substance" to mean faith is a literal substance. Kenneth Copeland called faith a "tangible force." Geisler replies that the Greek *hypostasis* means "assurance" or "confidence," so the verse is about being sure God will keep his promises.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_111-2

**v. 2**
- **Wesley:** God gave testimony both about and to the "elders" (the forefathers), and they received it as if it were the thing itself. He calls the chapter a summary of the Old Testament. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm
- **Guzik:** The original readers were discouraged Jewish Christians tempted to give up on Jesus, and these examples were meant to lift them out of discouragement.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-11/

**v. 3**
- **Wesley:** God created by his command alone, "without any instrument or preceding matter." Faith in creation is the foundation and model of all faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm
- **Guzik:**
  - We know creation by faith, and also by reason.
  - Against the common view of the time that the world was made from existing matter, the text says it was not made from visible things. 
  - The verse does not say God created *by* faith, since God sees everything and hopes for nothing. This is the opposite of Copeland's claim, quoted under v. 1, that faith was the raw material God used to make the universe. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_111-2
  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-11/

**v. 4**
- **Wesley:** Abel's faith was in the future Redeemer. His firstling offering confessed what his sins deserved, while Cain's offering was a bare acknowledgment of God as Creator. God probably showed approval by sending fire on the sacrifice. Abel "still speaks" that sinners are accepted only through faith in the great sacrifice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm
- **Guzik:** The difference was not animal versus vegetable but faith. He quotes Calvin (Reformed) agreeing. Abel's example shows that faith isn't always rewarded on earth.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-11/

**v. 5**
- **Wesley:** People may have searched for Enoch as they later did for Elijah. He had the testimony of pleasing God "in his own conscience." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm
- **Guzik:** Enoch is a mystery figure. Jude calls him a prophet, but the value of other prophecies credited to him is uncertain. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-11/

**v. 6**
- **Wesley:** Without "some divine faith in God" it is impossible to please him. "Comes to God" means in prayer or worship. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm
- **Guzik:** Two things are required: believe that God exists, and believe he rewards those who seek him. The text says "impossible," not "difficult."  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-11/

**v. 7**
- **Wesley:** Noah's open act of building the ark condemned a world that "neither believed nor feared." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm
- **Guzik:** Real faith always *does* something. Noah condemned the world by his conduct, not by preaching condemnation.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-11/

**v. 8**
- **Guzik:** Comparing Genesis 12 with Acts 7 shows Abraham first went only half way, yet God remembers his faith, not his delayed obedience.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-11/

**v. 9**
- **Wesley:** Isaac and Jacob showed the same faith by living the same way. Each received the inheritance from God, not from his father. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm
- **Guzik:** "Dwelt" means living as a resident alien, and Christians shouldn't live as permanent residents of earth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-11/

**v. 10**
- **Wesley:** A city with foundations, "whereas a tent has none." God alone designs, builds and finishes it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm
- **Clarke:** Abraham knew earth could give no permanent home to an immortal mind, so he kept heaven in view.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/11-10.html

**v. 11**
- **Wesley:** Sarah believed even though she had laughed at first (Gen. 18:12). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm
- **Guzik:** She went from laughing in unbelief to laughing in faith. God gave the strength, and she received it by faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-11/

**v. 12**
- **Wesley:** Abraham was "as good as dead" until God supernaturally restored his strength, which lasted for many years afterwards. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm

**v. 13**
- **Wesley:** "In death faith acts most vigorously." They embraced the promises "as one does a dear friend." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm
- **Guzik, citing Spurgeon (Baptist):** "Embraced" means "saluted," as when you greet a friend at a distance. Believers don't have faith to escape death, but to die in faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-11/

**vv. 14–15**
- **Wesley:** They longed for their true home. If they had missed Ur, they could easily have gone back. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm

**v. 16**
- **Wesley:** This is "a full convincing proof" that the patriarchs had a promise of eternal glory in heaven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm
- **Guzik:** Faith is hard when we live as "practical atheists." There is a sense in which God can be ashamed to be called our God when we don't treat heaven as real. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/studyguide_hbr/hbr_11.cfm

**v. 17**
- **Guzik:** The verb tense shows that, in Abraham's will and purpose, the sacrifice was complete.  Isaac is called "only begotten" because God did not count Ishmael. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/studyguide_hbr/hbr_11.cfm
- **Wesley:** Similarly, God accepted the will as if Abraham had actually done it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm

**v. 18**
- **Wesley:** "From him shall the blessed seed spring." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm

**v. 19**
- **Wesley:** Abraham believed in resurrection even though no one had yet been raised. "In a sense" means figuratively: Isaac was snatched from the jaws of death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm
- **Guzik:** Abraham obeyed the command and left God to keep the promise.  Receiving Isaac back prefigured Jesus' resurrection. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/studyguide_hbr/hbr_11.cfm

**v. 20**
- **Wesley:** Isaac prophetically foretold each son's blessings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm
- **Guzik:** Isaac acted from the flesh when he meant to bless Esau. He came to faith when he "trembled exceedingly," realising he had tried to defeat God's plan.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-11/

**v. 21** *(a point of difference)*
- **The text issue:**
  - Hebrews quotes the Septuagint (Greek Old Testament) of Gen. 47:31, "staff," where the Hebrew has "bed." The two words share the same consonants and differ only in later vowel marks.  https://bible.org/seriespage/hebrews-11
  - Calvin (Reformed) took this as evidence that ancient Hebrew had no vowel points.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/11-21.html
- **Against an old Catholic reading:**
  - Gill (Baptist) rejects the Latin Vulgate's "worshipped the top of his staff," which he says would be idolatry, not faith.  https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/hnv/hebrews/11-21.html
  - Matthew Henry dismisses "the papists'" idea of an image on the staff and sees the staff as a sign of Jacob's weakness.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_011.cfm
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown note that Jerome rejected the view that Jacob bowed to Joseph's staff. The Pulpit Commentary says some Church Fathers held that view but it has "little probability" and Augustine opposed it.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/11-21.htm
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** Moses and Hebrews are both right, because Jacob sat on the bed and leaned on his staff.  https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/jacob-worshipping-on-his-staff

**v. 22**
- **Wesley:** Joseph wanted his bones carried into the promised land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm
- **Guzik:** Joseph's unburied coffin was a silent witness for about 400 years that Israel would return. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/studyguide_hbr/hbr_11.cfm

**v. 23**
- **Wesley:** His parents saw the child "doubtless with a divine presage of things to come." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm
- **Guzik:** Faith gave them courage to obey God rather than man.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-11/

**vv. 24–25**
- **Guzik:** Moses let God, not Pharaoh, chart his future. Sin has real pleasures, but Moses saw they were passing.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-11/

**v. 26**
- **Wesley:** "Disgrace for Christ" is what Moses bore for believing in the Messiah to come. His reward was heaven, not Canaan. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm
- **Guzik:** Moses probably didn't know it then, but his suffering put him in Jesus' company. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/studyguide_hbr/hbr_11.cfm

**v. 27**
- **Wesley:** This is the Exodus. Moses was not afraid now, as he had been years earlier (Ex. 2:14). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm
- **Guzik:** His eye of faith saw that God was a bigger fact than Pharaoh's danger. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/studyguide_hbr/hbr_11.cfm

**v. 28**
- **Guzik:** Those who didn't trust in the Passover lamb's blood lost their firstborn.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-11/

**v. 29**
- **Guzik:** The difference between Israel and Egypt was not courage but faith.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-11/
- **Wesley:** From here on, the examples come from the Prophets rather than Genesis and Exodus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm

**vv. 30–31**
- **Wesley:** The walls fell "by the faith of Joshua." Rahab was "formerly one not of the fairest character." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm

**v. 32**
- **Wesley:** David was a prophet as well as a king. "The prophets" means Elijah, Elisha and the believers around them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm

**vv. 33–34**
- **Wesley matches the phrases to people:**
  - David conquered kingdoms.
  - Samuel administered justice.
  - Daniel shut the lions' mouths.
  - The three friends quenched the fire.
  - Then, in reverse order: Jephthah escaped the sword, Samson gained strength from weakness, Barak became mighty in battle, and Gideon routed armies.

  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm

**v. 35** *(a point of difference)*
- **Wesley:** The women are those whose sons were raised by Elijah and Elisha. The tortured refused release "on sinful terms," and the greater the suffering, the greater the glory. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm
- **Catholic view (catholic.com):** This is a clear reference to the seven brothers martyred in 2 Maccabees 7. Since that story appears nowhere in the Protestant Old Testament, the writer of Hebrews was using the deuterocanonical books (the books in Catholic but not Protestant Bibles).  https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/how-to-defend-the-deuterocanonicals
- **Protestant reply (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, on Bible Hub):** The writer of 2 Maccabees disclaims inspiration himself, so the allusion doesn't make the Apocrypha inspired.  Barnes thinks Eleazar's story (2 Macc. 6) was probably in view. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hebrews/11-35.htm
- **Guzik:** Those who suffered (vv. 35b–38) were as victorious through faith as those who conquered.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-11/

**vv. 36–38**
- **Wesley:** Here the writer turns to more recent examples. Jewish tradition says Isaiah was sawn in two by Manasseh. "The world was not worthy" means it didn't deserve such a blessing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm

**vv. 39–40**
- **Wesley:** They did not receive the great promise, the heavenly inheritance. The "something better" is everlasting glory, so that "we might all be perfected together in heaven." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/11.htm
- **Guzik:** They died without seeing the Messiah, and we have received him, so we have even more reason to keep going.  He quotes Leon Morris: only Christ's work brings Old and New Testament believers alike into God's presence.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-11/
